claims.text: Increasing the nanoindentation hardness-to-reduced-modulus ratio (Hn/Er) improves the wear resistance of HEA coatings.
A higher Hn/Er ratio indicates greater resistance to plastic deformation and abrasive damage during sliding.
The baseline HEA coating has a lower Hn/Er ratio and consequently only moderate hardness and wear resistance.
Increasing Ti content in a CoCrFeMnNi-based coating can be used to increase Hn/Er.
Controlled annealing can refine the coating microstructure and increase Hn/Er.
The proposed relationship should apply under dry sliding and more generally under abrasive, adhesive, or cavitation wear conditions.
The modified coating will have a refined microstructure with smaller grains and a denser dislocation network.
Smaller grains and a denser dislocation network increase hardness without a proportional increase in elastic modulus.
A higher Hn/Er ratio allows the coating to accommodate local contact stresses with less plastic deformation.
Reduced plastic flow under load causes less material removal and therefore lower wear.
Reduced plastic flow under load also lowers the coefficient of friction.
Coatings modified to have higher Hn/Er will exhibit lower wear volumes than the baseline.
Coatings modified to have higher Hn/Er will exhibit lower friction coefficients than the baseline.
The wear benefit should persist across sliding conditions typical of wear-resistant applications.
At extreme temperatures, very high loads, or under tribochemically dominated wear, Hn/Er may cease to govern wear performance.
Changes in operating conditions or composition can produce transitions among adhesive, abrasive, fatigue, and oxidative wear mechanisms.
The relationship between Ti content and wear performance can be nonmonotonic.
The magnitude and universality of the Hn/Er effect across HEA compositions, wear modes, and test conditions are uncertain.

contradictions.description: Increasing Ti is presented as an example modification expected to improve Hn/Er and wear performance, while the cited Ti-series result is explicitly nonmonotonic: friction and wear first decrease and then increase. The hypothesis does not specify the Ti range over which its intended modification is expected to be beneficial.
